title: Three chains under one roof, and the stores that undersold them
lede: FAO Inc. put three specialty chains together to serve what its chief executive called “the same affluent customer.”[^11] All three were sold or liquidated within two years.

blocks.title: FAO Inc.’s three brands, a later owner and a competitor
blocks.subtitle: Store counts are from FAO Inc.’s filings.

items.name: FAO Schwarz
items.text: Then two stores after the January 2004 sale, and none after July 2015. The name was revived in 2018.[^1][^2][^8][^22][^29]

items.name: Zany Brainy
items.text: Bought out of bankruptcy in September 2001. Same-store sales fell 17.9% in fiscal 2002.[^1][^2][^7]

items.name: The Right Start
items.text: The original business, founded as a catalog in 1985. Sold to Hancock Park Capital for about $5.4M.[^1][^2][^8]

items.name: Toys “R” Us
items.text: Hired FAO Schwarz’s chief executive in 2000, bought the brand in 2009, closed its last store in 2015 and sold it in 2016.[^9][^20][^22][^24][^29]

items.name: Wal-Mart
items.text: The discounter the press named in both bankruptcies as selling some of the same toys for less.[^13][^14]

blocks.source: FAO Inc. 10-K reports and 8-K[^1][^2][^7][^8]; Associated Press and Publishers Weekly[^13][^14][^29]. That Walmart is still operating is general knowledge. Whether the Zany Brainy and Right Start names have been used since is outside the scope of this page.

blocks.text: I think consumers were spending less on upscale toy retail products.
blocks.who: Maria Weiskott, editor-in-chief of Playthings, quoted by Publishers Weekly from Reuters, January 27, 2003[^12]
